text_blocks.snippet: Body rashes in adults can stem from various causes, including allergies, infections, skin conditions, or irritants. They can appear as red, itchy, swollen, or blistered areas and vary widely in appearance and severity. Seeking medical attention is advised for rashes that are painful, widespread, blistering, accompanied by fever, or persist without improvement after a few days.
snippet_highlighted_words: can stem from various causes, including allergies, infections, skin conditions, or irritants

list.title: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis):
list.snippet: A chronic condition causing red, itchy, and sometimes scaly skin, often associated with allergies or asthma.

list.title: Contact Dermatitis:
list.snippet: A rash caused by direct contact with an irritant or allergen, like certain soaps, cosmetics, or plants.

list.title: Shingles:
list.snippet: A reactivation of the chickenpox virus causing painful, blistering rash, often on one side of the body.

list.title: Cellulitis:
list.snippet: A bacterial skin infection causing red, swollen, and painful rash, requiring prompt medical attention.

list.title: Pityriasis Rosea:
list.snippet: A rash that typically starts with a single, larger patch (herald patch) and then spreads with smaller, scaly patches.

list.title: Rosacea:
list.snippet: A chronic condition causing redness, visible blood vessels, and sometimes small, red, pus-filled bumps, primarily on the face.

list.title: Viral Rashes:
list.snippet: Infections like measles, rubella, or fifth disease can cause characteristic rashes along with other symptoms.

list.title: Allergic Reactions:
list.snippet: Reactions to medications, food, or environmental allergens can manifest as rashes.

list.title: Bacterial Infections:
list.snippet: Certain bacterial infections can cause skin rashes, sometimes with pus, crusting, or pain.

list.title: Irritants:
list.snippet: Exposure to harsh chemicals, fabrics, or even some skincare products can trigger rashes.
Widespread rash: If a rash covers a large portion of the body.
Blistering or open sores: If the rash develops blisters or open sores.
Signs of infection: Pus, yellow or golden crusts, swelling, pain, or warmth around the rash, or fever.
Rapidly spreading rash: If the rash is spreading quickly.
Painful rash: If the rash is painful or causes significant discomfort.
Rash involving eyes, mouth, or genitals: If the rash affects these sensitive areas.
Rash accompanied by fever or illness:
Rash that doesn't improve with home care within a few days: If over-the-counter treatments are not effective.
Identify and avoid triggers: If the rash is related to an allergy or irritant, identify and avoid the trigger.
Keep the area clean: Gently cleanse with mild soap and pat dry.
Moisturize: Use a fragrance-free moisturizer to keep the skin hydrated.
Cool compresses: Apply cool, wet compresses to soothe inflammation and itching.
Over-the-counter treatments: Consider using hydrocortisone cream (1%) or oral antihistamines for itching.
